questions.q: Which issue was the main obstacle to an armistice during the talks that dragged on from 1951 to 1953?
options: Where to locate the permanent capital of Korea
Whether prisoners of war could refuse repatriation
Whether Japan would owe reparations to both Korean governments
How many U.S. troops would stay in Korea
questions.explain: The UN side insisted that POWs not be forced to return home, while the Communist side demanded forced repatriation. The dispute delayed the agreement for more than a year.

questions.q: NSC-68, a secret 1950 national security document, recommended what Cold War strategy?
options: A large peacetime military buildup to contain communism
A return to isolationism and rapid military demobilization
Immediate rollback of Soviet control in Eastern Europe
Reducing the defense budget to fund domestic programs
questions.explain: NSC-68 urged a major expansion of defense spending and of conventional and nuclear forces. The Korean War helped win acceptance for its approach.

questions.q: Executive Order 9981 (1948) shaped the integration of the units that fought in Korea. What did it do?
options: It created the Women's Army Corps as a permanent unit
It established the first peacetime draft lottery
It ended the Selective Service system after the war
It ordered equal treatment and opportunity in the armed forces
questions.explain: Truman's July 1948 order called for equal treatment and opportunity regardless of race, and the services were largely integrated during the Korean War.

questions.q: Which pair of 1949 events heightened American Cold War fears just before the Korean War?
options: The Marshall Plan and the Truman Doctrine
The Cuban Revolution and the Bay of Pigs
The Soviet atomic bomb test and the Communist victory in China
The launch of Sputnik and the shootdown of a U-2
questions.explain: The USSR exploded its first atomic bomb in August 1949 and Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China in October 1949.

questions.q: The Korean War Veterans Memorial features 19 stainless steel statues of soldiers walking beside a granite wall. What does that mural wall display?
options: The names of all U.S. casualties
Etched images from photographs of Korean War service members
Maps of every major battle of the war
questions.explain: The Mural Wall carries over 2,400 photographic images, based on National Archives photos, sandblasted into granite. The memorial was dedicated in 1995.

questions.q: What words are inscribed in the granite near the Pool of Remembrance at the Korean War Veterans Memorial?
questions.explain: The phrase "Freedom Is Not Free" is carved at the memorial, reminding visitors of the cost of defending South Korea.

questions.q: What agreement did the United States sign with South Korea in October 1953, shortly after the armistice?
options: A treaty ending the occupation of Korea
questions.explain: The U.S.-South Korea Mutual Defense Treaty, signed in Washington on October 1, 1953, says each side would act to meet an armed attack on the other, and it underlies the continuing U.S. troop presence.

questions.q: The Korean War is often described as the first major test of containment. Which 1947 policy first articulated this approach by pledging aid to Greece and Turkey?
questions.explain: The Truman Doctrine pledged U.S. support for free peoples resisting subjugation, first applied to Greece and Turkey. Korea extended containment to Asia.

questions.q: In an April 1951 address to Congress, MacArthur said, "Old soldiers never die; they just fade away." What prompted the speech?
options: His retirement after reaching the mandatory age of 65
His appointment as Army Chief of Staff
His removal from command by President Truman
questions.explain: MacArthur spoke to a joint session of Congress on April 19, 1951, defending his proposals for a wider war against China and ending his career with this farewell line.

questions.q: The Tet Offensive of January 1968 had what major effect on American public opinion?
options: It convinced most Americans that victory was near
It undermined confidence in official claims that the war was being won
It ended the draft immediately and brought home all troops
It brought China openly into the war
questions.explain: Although the offensive was a military defeat for Communist forces, its scale contradicted optimistic reports and deepened public doubts about the war.

questions.q: In New York Times Co. v. United States (1971), the Supreme Court allowed publication of the Pentagon Papers. Which principle did the ruling reflect?
options: A strong presumption against prior restraint
That classified documents become public property once leaked
That newspapers may publish anything without later penalty
That Congress controls what newspapers may publish
questions.explain: The Court held that the government had not met its heavy burden to justify blocking publication in advance of the secret Vietnam War study.

questions.q: On March 31, 1968, Lyndon Johnson stunned the nation by announcing that he would do what?
questions.explain: After Tet and a close New Hampshire primary, Johnson announced a partial bombing halt and said he would neither seek nor accept his party's nomination.

questions.q: In 1945 Ho Chi Minh opened Vietnam's declaration of independence by quoting which American document?
questions.explain: On September 2, 1945, Ho Chi Minh began by citing that all men are created equal, hoping for U.S. sympathy against returning French rule.

questions.q: What military personnel policy, in effect from 1994, was repealed by Congress in 2010?
questions.explain: The policy barred openly gay people from military service while forbidding commanders from asking about orientation. Repeal took effect in September 2011.

questions.q: The Posse Comitatus Act of 1878 restricts what use of the military within the United States?
options: Stationing troops in any city of more than 100,000 people
Drafting civilians into the army during peacetime
Selling surplus military weapons to the state governments
Using troops to enforce civilian law without authorization
questions.explain: Passed as Reconstruction ended, the act limits the federal military's role in domestic law enforcement.

questions.q: The Women's Armed Services Integration Act of 1948 did what?
options: Created the Women's Army Corps for the first time
Required equal pay in the services
Made women permanent members of the regular armed forces
questions.explain: Signed by Truman, the law gave women regular and reserve status, though with limits such as a two percent cap on their numbers.

questions.q: What change to military service took effect in 1973 as the Vietnam War ended?
options: Women were drafted for the first time
The draft age was lowered to 17
The draft ended and the all-volunteer force began
questions.explain: Draft authority expired in mid-1973 and the nation moved to an all-volunteer military, as recommended by the Gates Commission.

questions.q: The Defense Department created the Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA) in 1958 in response to what event?
options: The construction of the Berlin Wall
questions.explain: ARPA, now DARPA, funded research that later produced ARPANET, forerunner of the internet.

questions.q: The Goldwater-Nichols Act of 1986 reorganized the Pentagon chiefly by doing what?
options: Strengthening joint command and the role of the Joint Chiefs chairman
Merging the Army and Navy into a single service
Moving the Defense Department under Congress
questions.explain: The law reduced interservice rivalry, making the chairman the principal military adviser to the president and strengthening combatant commanders.

questions.q: The Woolworth lunch counter on display at the National Museum of American History comes from which city, where students began sit-ins on February 1, 1960?
options: Selma, Alabama, site of the 1965 marches
questions.explain: Four North Carolina A&T students sat at the Greensboro Woolworth counter, sparking a wave of sit-ins across the South.

questions.q: Who dedicated the National Museum of African American History and Culture in September 2016?
questions.explain: Obama spoke at the museum's dedication on September 24, 2016, on the National Mall, after years of effort to create a national museum of Black history.

questions.q: Which president signed the 2003 law establishing the National Museum of African American History and Culture?
questions.explain: The National Museum of African American History and Culture Act was signed in December 2003 after decades of advocacy, including by Representative John Lewis.

questions.q: Which Reconstruction-era amendment declared that all persons born in the United States are citizens and guaranteed equal protection of the laws?
questions.explain: Ratified in 1868, it overturned Dred Scott's denial of citizenship and became the basis of later civil rights litigation.

questions.q: In 1941 A. Philip Randolph's threatened March on Washington led President Roosevelt to issue Executive Order 8802, which did what?
options: Integrated all branches of the armed forces
Banned discrimination in defense jobs and created the Fair Employment Practice Committee
Ended segregation in public schools in the South
Outlawed the poll tax in federal elections
questions.explain: Roosevelt acted in June 1941 to head off the march; the order barred discrimination in defense industries and set up the Fair Employment Practice Committee.

questions.q: Booker T. Washington's 1895 Atlanta Compromise speech differed from W. E. B. Du Bois's later program in that Washington urged Black Americans to do what?
options: Focus on vocational training and economic progress before demanding political equality
Leave the South and emigrate to Africa to build new nations
Reject education altogether in favor of farm labor
Demand immediate integration through protest and the vote
questions.explain: Du Bois, in The Souls of Black Folk (1903), criticized this approach and called for full civil rights and a college-educated 'Talented Tenth.'

questions.q: In Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857), Chief Justice Roger Taney wrote that people of African descent could not be what?
questions.explain: The Court ruled that Black Americans, free or enslaved, were not citizens and that Congress could not bar slavery from the territories.

questions.q: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 followed national outrage over events in which city?
questions.explain: Violence against marchers on "Bloody Sunday" in Selma in March 1965 helped persuade Congress to pass the Voting Rights Act that August.

questions.q: Historian Carter G. Woodson started Negro History Week in 1926, which later became what?
questions.explain: Woodson founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History in 1915; the weeklong observance grew into Black History Month, recognized by President Ford in 1976.

questions.q: The Wounded Knee Massacre of December 1890 involved U.S. Army troops and which group?
questions.explain: U.S. cavalry killed hundreds of Lakota, including many women and children, at Wounded Knee Creek, South Dakota, on December 29, 1890.

questions.q: The Spanish brought which animal to the Americas, transforming Plains Indian life after Native peoples acquired it?
questions.explain: Horses reached Plains nations through Spanish colonial trade and raiding, enabling more effective bison hunting and travel.

questions.q: Native activists occupied which island in San Francisco Bay from 1969 to 1971 to draw attention to Native rights?
questions.explain: The occupation by Indians of All Tribes raised national awareness and helped lead to a shift toward federal support for self-determination.

questions.q: The Proclamation of 1763 forbade colonists from settling where?
options: North of the Ohio River and west of Lake Erie
questions.explain: Issued in October 1763 while Pontiac's War was under way, it tried to reduce conflict with Native nations but angered colonists.

questions.q: Charles Lindbergh's May 1927 flight in the Spirit of St. Louis was the first solo nonstop flight between which two cities?
questions.explain: The flight of about 33 hours made Lindbergh a worldwide celebrity and spurred interest in aviation.

questions.q: The Soviet launch of what satellite on October 4, 1957 alarmed Americans and began the space race?
questions.explain: Sputnik 1 was the first artificial satellite; the United States responded with NASA (1958) and the National Defense Education Act.

questions.q: In a May 1961 speech to Congress, President Kennedy set what national goal?
options: Landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely before the decade ended
Orbiting a permanent space station by 1965
Sending astronauts around Mars before the decade ended
Building a permanent lunar base by 1970
questions.explain: Kennedy asked Congress to fund landing a man on the Moon and returning him safely to Earth before 1970, a goal met by Apollo 11 in July 1969.

questions.q: Who in 1947 piloted the Bell X-1 and became the first person to fly faster than the speed of sound?
questions.explain: Yeager broke the sound barrier on October 14, 1947; the aircraft, named Glamorous Glennis, is displayed at the National Air and Space Museum.

questions.q: The Enola Gay, now displayed by the National Air and Space Museum, dropped an atomic bomb on which Japanese city on August 6, 1945?
questions.explain: The B-29 bomber dropped the first atomic bomb used in war; a second fell on Nagasaki three days later.

questions.q: The 1975 Apollo-Soyuz Test Project was significant as a symbol of what?
options: Soviet victory in the race to reach the Moon
Cold War detente through a joint U.S.-Soviet space mission
questions.explain: American and Soviet spacecraft docked in orbit in July 1975, a high point of detente.

questions.q: The April 1942 Doolittle Raid was notable as the first U.S. air raid to strike what?
questions.explain: Sixteen B-25 bombers launched from the USS Hornet struck Tokyo and other cities, boosting American morale after Pearl Harbor.

questions.q: After Lincoln's assassination, the conspirators were tried by a military commission. Which 1866 Supreme Court case later held that military trials of civilians are unconstitutional where civilian courts are open?
questions.explain: Milligan, decided in 1866, limited military tribunals for civilians, though the conspirators' trial had already taken place in 1865.

questions.q: The Tenure of Office Act (1867), which led to Johnson's impeachment, restricted what presidential power?
options: The power to veto bills passed by Congress
The power to command the army in time of war
The power to remove certain officials without Senate approval
The power to grant pardons for federal offenses
questions.explain: Johnson violated the act by dismissing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton without Senate consent.

questions.q: On the night of Lincoln's assassination, a conspirator also attacked which cabinet member at his home?
options: Secretary of the Treasury Hugh McCulloch
questions.explain: Lewis Powell stabbed Seward, who survived. Plans to kill Vice President Johnson were not carried out.

questions.q: In 1865 Mary Surratt became the first woman to be executed by the federal government after being convicted of what?
options: Conspiring in the plot to kill Lincoln
Spying for the Union army in Maryland and Virginia
questions.explain: Surratt ran the Washington boarding house where conspirators met. She was hanged July 7, 1865, the first woman executed by the federal government.

questions.q: The Compromise of 1790 traded what for locating the national capital on the Potomac River?
options: A ban on the slave trade
Southern support for the federal assumption of state debts
questions.explain: Hamilton, Jefferson and Madison reportedly agreed that Southern votes for assumption would be traded for a capital in the South.

questions.q: Alexander Hamilton defended the constitutionality of the First Bank of the United States using which clause?
options: The supremacy clause of Article VI
questions.explain: Hamilton argued for implied powers, while Jefferson favored a strict reading. Washington signed the bank bill in 1791.

questions.q: Andrew Jackson's Bank War led him in 1833 to do what?
options: Remove federal deposits from the Second Bank and place them in state banks
questions.explain: Jackson removed federal deposits from the Bank in 1833 and distributed them to state banks, which opponents condemned as an abuse of executive power.

questions.q: The 1794 Whiskey Rebellion arose in opposition to what federal policy?
options: A ban on distilling whiskey in western Pennsylvania
An excise tax on distilled spirits
questions.explain: Western Pennsylvania distillers resisted the 1791 tax. Washington led a militia force against them, showing that the federal government would enforce its laws.

questions.q: Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau Jr. helped lead U.S. participation in which 1944 conference that created the IMF and World Bank?
questions.explain: Delegates at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, created the IMF and the World Bank in 1944. Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau presided over the conference.

questions.q: In 1865 the Secret Service was created within the Treasury Department primarily to do what?
questions.explain: Created in 1865 to fight counterfeiting, the Secret Service stayed in the Treasury Department until 2003 and began protecting presidents after McKinley's assassination in 1901.

questions.q: Douglass quarreled with Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Susan B. Anthony in 1869 because he supported which amendment even though it did not enfranchise women?
questions.explain: Stanton and Anthony opposed the amendment because it did not include women, while Douglass backed it. The movement split into rival groups until the 1890s.

questions.q: In the Civil War, Douglass recruited Black soldiers, including two of his sons, for which regiment?
questions.explain: Douglass recruited Black soldiers for the 54th Massachusetts, and his sons Lewis and Charles enlisted in it; Lewis became its sergeant major, while Charles later served in the 5th Massachusetts Cavalry. It was one of the first Black regiments raised in the North.

questions.q: Douglass held which federal appointment after Hayes took office in 1877?
options: U.S. Marshal for the District of Columbia
questions.explain: President Hayes appointed Douglass U.S. Marshal for the District of Columbia in 1877; he later served as Recorder of Deeds and as Minister to Haiti.

questions.q: Douglass delivered the keynote at the 1876 dedication of the Freedmen's Memorial in Washington to whom?
questions.explain: Douglass spoke at the unveiling of the Freedmen's Monument in Washington on April 14, 1876, offering a mixed assessment of Lincoln.

questions.q: The Compromise of 1877 resolved the disputed election of 1876 and led to what?
options: Withdrawal of federal troops from the South, ending Reconstruction
Impeachment of Hayes by the House of Representatives
A convention to write a new national constitution
Ratification of the Fifteenth Amendment that spring
questions.explain: In exchange for Democrats accepting Hayes's disputed victory, Republicans ended military oversight of the South; Hayes withdrew the federal troops guarding the South Carolina and Louisiana statehouses.

questions.q: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his final Sunday sermon at Washington National Cathedral four days before his death. What was the date?
questions.explain: He preached "Remaining Awake Through a Great Revolution" on March 31, 1968.

questions.q: The First Amendment's religion clauses prohibit Congress from doing what?
options: Establishing a religion or prohibiting its free exercise
questions.explain: The Establishment Clause bars government from setting up a church, and the Free Exercise Clause protects the right to practice religion.

questions.q: The Second Great Awakening, beginning around 1800, led to what?
options: The end of Protestant denominations in the United States
A wave of opposition to all reform movements
Revivals and reform movements such as abolitionism and temperance
The creation of official state churches in every state
questions.explain: Camp meetings such as Cane Ridge (1801) spread evangelical revivals, which fueled antebellum reforms such as temperance and abolitionism.

questions.q: In 1954 Congress added which words to the Pledge of Allegiance during the Cold War?
questions.explain: Added in 1954 during the Cold War, the words distinguished the United States from the state atheism of communist countries.

questions.q: Which colony passed the 1649 Act of Toleration protecting Trinitarian Christians?
questions.explain: Passed in 1649 under Cecil Calvert's proprietorship, the act is often cited as the first colonial law protecting religious toleration for Christians, though it excluded those who denied the Trinity.

questions.q: The Great Awakening of the 1740s featured which English preacher who toured the colonies?
questions.explain: English preacher George Whitefield drew huge crowds across the colonies in the 1740s, helping to spread the Great Awakening.

questions.q: Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971) produced a test for what?
options: Whether a law violates the Establishment Clause
questions.explain: In Lemon v. Kurtzman (1971) the Court set a three-part test: a law needs a secular purpose, must not advance or inhibit religion, and must avoid excessive entanglement.

questions.q: Which agency took over operation of U.S. railroads during World War I?
questions.explain: To keep trains moving for the war effort, the federal government took over the railroads on December 28, 1917, and returned them to their owners in 1920.

questions.q: The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 targeted immigrants who had helped build which railroad?
questions.explain: Thousands of Chinese immigrants did much of the Central Pacific's construction work in the 1860s, yet the 1882 act barred new Chinese laborers.

questions.q: Plessy v. Ferguson arose from a challenge to a law requiring what?
options: Separate railway cars for Black and white passengers
Segregated public schools in every Louisiana parish
Segregated polling places for Black and white voters
Segregated housing in New Orleans neighborhoods
questions.explain: Homer Plessy deliberately sat in a whites-only car in Louisiana in 1892 to challenge the law, leading to the Supreme Court's 1896 decision.

questions.q: Which leader headed North Korea's Soviet-backed government when it invaded the South?
questions.explain: Kim Il Sung was installed by the Soviet Union as North Korea's leader after World War II and launched the 1950 invasion with Stalin's approval.

questions.q: Eisenhower's "New Look" defense policy of the 1950s relied heavily on what?
options: Nuclear weapons and the threat of massive retaliation
Limited wars fought only by allies
questions.explain: The New Look cut spending on conventional forces after Korea and stressed nuclear deterrence as a cheaper way to contain communism.

questions.q: In February 1950, which senator claimed to hold a list of Communists in the State Department, setting off a campaign that intensified during the Korean War?
questions.explain: McCarthy's Wheeling, West Virginia speech launched years of accusations. The loss of China and the Korean War heightened public fear of communism.

questions.q: In 1954 President Eisenhower described what idea to explain why the fall of Indochina to communism would matter?
questions.explain: At an April 1954 press conference Eisenhower likened the countries of Southeast Asia to falling dominoes. The idea guided U.S. policy toward Vietnam.

questions.q: What did Nixon announce on April 30, 1970, that sparked widespread campus protests?
options: Resumed bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong
A U.S. ground incursion into Cambodia
questions.explain: Nixon said troops would attack North Vietnamese sanctuaries in Cambodia. The announcement led to protests, including at Kent State and Jackson State.

questions.q: In his 1968 broadcast after the Tet Offensive, which respected television journalist said the war seemed "mired in stalemate"?
questions.explain: Cronkite's February 1968 report, after a trip to Vietnam, was widely seen as a sign that mainstream opinion was turning against the war.

questions.q: Frederick Douglass escaped slavery in Baltimore in September 1838. In which city did he first find shelter with the abolitionist David Ruggles?
questions.explain: Douglass traveled by train and steamboat through Philadelphia to New York in September 1838, where Ruggles sheltered him. He soon settled in New Bedford, Massachusetts.

questions.q: At the 1848 Seneca Falls convention, Douglass was one of few men to speak in favor of what?
options: A resolution to abolish slavery throughout the nation
A call for Black colonization in Africa
A resolution condemning the Mexican War and annexation
A resolution calling for women's right to vote
questions.explain: Douglass argued that women had the same claim to the vote as men; after heated debate, the suffrage resolution was the only one not passed unanimously.

questions.q: In 1859 John Brown asked Douglass to join his plan to seize the federal arsenal at which town?
questions.explain: Douglass declined, thinking the plan was doomed, and later left the country for a time.

questions.q: In 1874 Douglass briefly served as president of which institution founded to serve freed people?
questions.explain: The bank collapsed that year, wiping out the savings of many Black depositors.

questions.q: Which deafblind author and activist is entombed at Washington National Cathedral?
questions.explain: Helen Keller and her teacher Anne Sullivan are interred in the cathedral's Saint Joseph's Chapel.

questions.q: Whose 2018 state funeral service was held at Washington National Cathedral?
questions.explain: Bush's funeral on December 5, 2018 was one of several presidential state funerals held at the cathedral.

questions.q: Anne Hutchinson was banished from Massachusetts Bay in 1637 for what offense?
options: Challenging Puritan ministers' authority with her own religious teachings
questions.explain: Her claim of direct divine revelation, called antinomianism, threatened Puritan leaders; she then helped found a settlement in Rhode Island.

questions.q: King's 1963 "Letter from Birmingham Jail" was addressed mainly to whom?
options: White Alabama clergymen who had criticized the demonstrations
questions.explain: King responded to eight white clergymen who had called his protests "unwise and untimely."

questions.q: Which 1901-1902 plan for Washington led to the consolidation of railroad stations into a single Union Station off the National Mall?
questions.explain: The McMillan Commission, which included Daniel Burnham, proposed removing railroad tracks and stations from the Mall; Union Station opened in 1907.

questions.q: In Northern Securities Co. v. United States (1904), the Supreme Court ordered the breakup of a company controlling which industry?
questions.explain: The decision, a victory for Theodore Roosevelt's antitrust efforts, dissolved a railroad holding company assembled by J. P. Morgan and James J. Hill.

questions.q: John Wilkes Booth was killed in April 1865 at a farm in which state?
questions.explain: Union soldiers cornered Booth at Garrett's farm, near Port Royal, Virginia, on April 26.

questions.q: Henry Ford's moving assembly line, introduced in 1913, dramatically lowered the cost of making which car?
questions.explain: The assembly line cut the production time for a Model T from hours to just over an hour and a half, making cars affordable to more Americans.

questions.q: The Wright brothers' key innovation, which allowed pilots to control the aircraft in flight, was what?
options: A jet engine mounted in the fuselage
Wing warping combined with a movable rudder
questions.explain: They controlled roll with wing warping, a rudder and a front elevator, a three-axis control system.

questions.q: The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into orbit in 1990 aboard which vehicle?
questions.explain: Discovery carried Hubble into orbit on April 24, 1990, on mission STS-31.

questions.q: In a January 1950 speech, Secretary of State Dean Acheson described a U.S. "defensive perimeter" in the Pacific that left out which place, an omission some historians say encouraged the invasion?
questions.explain: Acheson's National Press Club speech did not list South Korea within the perimeter. Critics later argued the omission signaled that the United States would not defend it.

questions.q: Soon after North Korea invaded South Korea in June 1950, Truman ordered the U.S. Seventh Fleet into the Taiwan Strait. What was one purpose of this move?
options: To land marines at ports in northern Korea
To prevent a Communist invasion of Taiwan
questions.explain: The order of June 27, 1950 tied the Korean conflict to the Chinese Civil War and kept the Nationalist government on Taiwan out of Communist reach.

questions.q: Where did the first U.S. Marine combat units land in South Vietnam in March 1965?
questions.explain: Marines arrived at Da Nang on March 8, 1965, to defend the air base, marking the start of the U.S. ground war.

questions.q: SEATO, created in 1954 after the French defeat, was designed to do what?
options: Provide collective defense against communism in Southeast Asia
questions.explain: The Southeast Asia Treaty Organization gave the United States a basis for involvement in the region, though most members were not in Southeast Asia.

questions.q: In 1968, protesters clashed with Chicago police outside which party's national convention?
questions.explain: The turmoil in Chicago reflected the Democratic Party's division over Vietnam and added to the sense of national crisis in 1968.

questions.q: What body, created after Truman's Executive Order 9981, worked on integrating the armed forces?
questions.explain: The committee, headed by Charles Fahy, pressed the services to end racial quotas and segregated units.

questions.q: Which journalist's 1892 pamphlet Southern Horrors exposed the lynching of Black Americans?
questions.explain: Wells led a campaign against lynching after the killing of friends in Memphis, and showed that the usual justifications were false.

questions.q: The 1931 Scottsboro case involved nine Black teenagers falsely accused of rape in which state?
questions.explain: The case drew international attention; the Supreme Court overturned convictions in Powell v. Alabama (1932) because the youths lacked adequate counsel.

questions.q: Phillis Wheatley, who was born in Africa and enslaved in Boston, was notable for what accomplishment in 1773?
questions.explain: Her Poems on Various Subjects was one of the first books by an African American woman, and she was freed soon after.

questions.q: Who was the African American killed in the Boston Massacre of March 1770?
questions.explain: Attucks, of African and Native descent, is often considered the first casualty of the American Revolution.

questions.q: In 1841 the Supreme Court freed the captives of the Amistad. Which former president argued their case?
options: Martin Van Buren of New York
questions.explain: Adams argued that the captives had been illegally kidnapped and had a right to resist.

questions.q: Whose murder in Mississippi in 1955 galvanized the civil rights movement after his mother insisted on an open casket funeral?
questions.explain: Mamie Till wanted the world to see what had been done to her 14-year-old son, and photographs were published nationally.

questions.q: Samuel Morse's 1844 demonstration line connected the Capitol in Washington with which city?
questions.explain: The experimental line followed the Baltimore and Ohio railroad route.

questions.q: In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831), Chief Justice Marshall described Native nations as what?
questions.explain: Marshall held that the Cherokee were not a foreign nation entitled to sue in the Supreme Court, but a distinct political society in a relationship like that of a ward to a guardian.

questions.q: The 1795 Treaty of Greenville followed which battle in which General Anthony Wayne defeated a Native confederacy?
questions.explain: The treaty, signed in 1795, forced Native nations to cede much of present-day Ohio.

questions.q: The Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876 was a Lakota and Cheyenne victory over troops commanded by whom?
questions.explain: Custer and the roughly 210 men of his five companies were killed, though the rest of the 7th Cavalry under Reno and Benteen survived; the army responded with a campaign that forced the Lakota onto reservations.

questions.q: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce is remembered for saying at his 1877 surrender, "From where the sun now stands, I will fight no more forever." What led to his surrender?
options: A long retreat toward Canada pursued by U.S. troops
A smallpox epidemic that killed their leaders
questions.explain: The Nez Perce fled more than a thousand miles before being stopped near the Canadian border in Montana.

questions.q: The 1814 Battle of Horseshoe Bend, in which Andrew Jackson defeated Red Stick Creeks, was followed by a treaty requiring the Creek to do what?
options: Cede millions of acres, including land of Creek allies
questions.explain: The Treaty of Fort Jackson took about 23 million acres, much of it from Creeks who had sided with Jackson.

questions.q: House Concurrent Resolution 108 (1953) launched what federal policy toward Native nations?
options: Termination of federal recognition and services
Expansion of reservations across the West
questions.explain: The resolution aimed to end the special federal relationship with tribes; together with a companion program that relocated Native people to cities, termination proved disastrous for many tribes.

questions.q: What happened aboard Apollo 13 in April 1970?
options: The crew was stranded on the Moon
An oxygen tank exploded, forcing the crew to abort the Moon landing
questions.explain: The crew used the lunar module as a lifeboat and returned safely to Earth.

questions.q: The first woman in space, in 1963, was a citizen of which country?
questions.explain: Valentina Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times aboard Vostok 6; the first American woman did not fly until 1983.

questions.q: Billy Mitchell was court-martialed in 1925 for what?
options: Publicly accusing military leaders of negligence in air power policy
questions.explain: Mitchell, an advocate of air power, was found guilty of insubordination, but later events vindicated many of his ideas.

questions.q: Katherine Johnson, an African American mathematician at NASA, is best known for doing what?
options: Designing the rocket engines for Apollo
Calculating trajectories for early crewed spaceflights
questions.explain: Johnson, an African American mathematician, calculated orbital paths for Mercury and Apollo missions.

questions.q: Lincoln's December 1863 Reconstruction proclamation allowed a Southern state to form a new government when what share of its 1860 voters swore loyalty?
questions.explain: Lincoln's proclamation offered pardons and let states rejoin once 10 percent of 1860 voters took the oath and accepted emancipation.

questions.q: Robert F. Kennedy, buried at Arlington in 1968, was assassinated shortly after winning the Democratic primary in which state?
questions.explain: Kennedy was shot on June 5, 1968, in Los Angeles and died the next day.

questions.q: Robert E. Lee resigned from the U.S. Army in April 1861 after which event?
options: The firing on Fort Sumter alone
Lincoln's call for slaves to enlist
questions.explain: Lee declined command of the Union army and left his Arlington home when Virginia seceded.

questions.q: Hamilton's 1791 Report on Manufactures proposed what policy?
options: Tariffs and subsidies to encourage American industry
questions.explain: Hamilton argued that government support would diversify the economy; Congress rejected his proposed bounties, though it adopted many of his tariff recommendations in 1792.

questions.q: The 1828 "Tariff of Abominations" led to a crisis in which Southern state?
questions.explain: South Carolina argued that the tariff was unconstitutional and nullified it in 1832, prompting a confrontation with Jackson.

questions.q: The Panic of 1907 led to the creation of which institution six years later?
questions.explain: J. P. Morgan helped stop the 1907 panic, convincing many that the nation needed a central banking authority.

questions.q: Which 1933 law, passed in the first days of the New Deal, let the Treasury reopen solvent banks after a bank holiday?
questions.explain: Congress passed it within hours of Franklin Roosevelt's request, helping restore confidence.

questions.q: What were Series E war bonds, sold by the Treasury during World War II?
options: Low-denomination bonds sold to ordinary Americans to finance the war
questions.explain: The Treasury marketed war bonds through rallies and posters to help finance the war and reduce inflation.

questions.q: The 1873 Panic was triggered in part by the failure of Jay Cooke and Company, which was financing which project?
questions.explain: Cooke's bank collapsed after overextending itself on railroad bonds, starting a long depression.

questions.q: The Railway Labor Act of 1926 was significant because it did what?
options: Protected railroad workers' right to organize and bargain
questions.explain: The act set procedures for mediation between railroads and unions and became a model for later labor law.

questions.q: The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, signed by Eisenhower, contributed to the decline of passenger rail by doing what?
options: Taxing train tickets to fund highways
Funding a national system of interstate highways
questions.explain: Cheap highway travel and air travel drew passengers away from the railroads, leading to Amtrak's creation in the 1970s.

questions.q: The funeral train of President Franklin D. Roosevelt in April 1945 first carried his body from Warm Springs, Georgia, to which city for a funeral service before burial elsewhere?
questions.explain: Roosevelt died April 12, 1945; his body went to Washington for a service and then to Hyde Park for burial.

questions.q: In a 1790 letter to a Rhode Island synagogue, Washington wrote that the government gives "to bigotry no sanction, to persecution no assistance." Which community did he address?
questions.explain: Washington assured the Jewish congregation of religious liberty as a natural right under the new government.

questions.q: Mary Dyer was hanged in Boston in 1660 for what reason?
options: She was convicted of witchcraft by a jury
She returned to Massachusetts after being banished as a Quaker
She sold firearms to Native Americans
questions.explain: Dyer was one of the four Quakers executed by Massachusetts, a case that helped drive demands for religious toleration.

questions.q: In Abington School District v. Schempp (1963), the Supreme Court held unconstitutional what practice?
options: Required Bible reading in public schools
Teaching about religion in literature classes
Opening sessions of Congress with prayer
questions.explain: The decision followed Engel v. Vitale (1962) in limiting government-sponsored religious exercises in public schools.

questions.q: In Wisconsin v. Yoder (1972), the Supreme Court ruled that Amish parents could do what?
options: Withdraw their children from school after eighth grade
questions.explain: The Court held that the Free Exercise Clause protected the Amish way of life from compulsory attendance laws.

questions.q: In Reynolds v. United States (1879), the Supreme Court held that the Free Exercise Clause did not protect what?
questions.explain: The Court distinguished religious belief, which is protected absolutely, from actions that can be regulated.

questions.q: Which reformer published The Woman's Bible in 1895, criticizing the use of scripture to subordinate women?
questions.explain: Stanton and a committee of women commented on passages that referred to women, angering many suffrage allies.

questions.q: The Moral Majority, founded in 1979, was an organization of what kind?
options: A conservative Christian political group led by Jerry Falwell
questions.explain: The group helped mobilize evangelical voters for Republican candidates, including Ronald Reagan in 1980.

questions.q: Which Philadelphia minister was elected the first bishop of the African Methodist Episcopal Church in 1816?
questions.explain: Allen left a segregated Methodist congregation and led the AME Church, one of the first independent Black denominations in the United States.

questions.q: In a 1960 speech to Protestant ministers in Houston, John F. Kennedy said he believed in an America where what was "absolute"?
options: The separation of church and state
The supremacy of federal law over state law
The privilege of the executive branch
questions.explain: Facing doubts about his Catholicism, Kennedy said he believed in an America where the separation of church and state is absolute.
